content.title: About
content.content: Rice paper are thin sheets made from rice flour, water and sometimes starch. Traditionally used in Southeast Asian cuisines for rolls, spring rolls and wraps, the paper has a soft, slightly elastic texture and a neutral taste that lets the filling shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice paper production began in Vietnam in the early 1920s.
It can be either translucent or milky‑white depending on the ratio of rice flour to starch.
Unlike traditional rice noodles, the sheets do not require cooking – a quick soak in warm water for 10–20 seconds is enough.
Some varieties include seaweed extracts, giving the paper a subtle marine aroma.
Crisped rice paper chips are a popular snack after a brief fry.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Rice paper contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich source of complex carbs
items.content: The main component is complex carbohydrates that provide a steady release of energy.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Made from pure rice flour, it is safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Contains small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice flour retains modest levels of thiamine and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The thin structure aids digestion, especially in light dishes.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice flour.

items.title: Sodium content in processed sheets
items.content: Some ready‑made sheets are salted; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can allow mold growth; keep the product in proper conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak the sheets in warm water for 10–20 seconds until pliable, then wrap fresh vegetables, seafood, meat or tofu. They can be quickly pan‑fried for a crisp edge or baked in the oven. As a snack, cut the sheets into strips and fry them to make rice chips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rice paper in an airtight package in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator, where it stays flexible for up to 6 months. Discard any sheets that develop a moldy smell or discoloration.
